summary.text: Optical rotation is the turning of the plane of polarization of linearly polarized light as it travels through certain materials.
It occurs only in chiral materials, and unlike other sources of birefringence it can be observed in fluids such as gases and solutions of chiral molecules.
The angle of rotation grows with the path length and, in a solution, with its concentration, so polarimeters can measure sugar concentration.

facts.label: Sugar industry use
facts.value: Polarimeters measure the sugar concentration of syrup

facts.label: Examples
facts.value: Sucrose and camphor turn light right; cholesterol turns it left

items.prompt: A polarimeter reads a certain angle for a sugar solution in a tube. You make the solution twice as concentrated and keep the same tube. What happens to the angle?

options.label: It stays the same
It shrinks
It becomes proportionally larger
It reverses direction

items.explain: For a solution the angle is proportional to its concentration, so doubling the concentration increases it in proportion.

items.prompt: A chiral molecule turns polarized light to the right by a certain angle. What does its mirror image do?

options.label: Turns it to the right by the same angle
Turns it to the left by the same angle
Turns it to the left by twice the angle
Does not turn it at all

items.explain: Enantiomers rotate plane-polarized light the same number of degrees, but in opposite directions.

items.prompt: A student reasons that every L-amino acid in proteins must turn polarized light to the left. What is wrong with that?

options.label: Proteins are built from no amino acids
The L label does not give the rotation direction
L always means a turn to the right
Amino acids never rotate any light

items.explain: The prefix for absolute configuration is not directly related to the (+) or (−) sign; some L-amino acids are dextrorotary.

items.prompt: A material has microscopic mirror symmetry. Will it show optical activity?

options.label: No, only chiral materials lacking such symmetry do
Yes, every liquid does
Yes, if the light is bright enough
Only if it is a solid crystal

items.explain: Optical activity occurs only in chiral materials, those lacking microscopic mirror symmetry.

items.prompt: Two quartz crystals have structures that are mirror images of each other. How do they treat linearly polarized light?

options.label: Both turn it the same way by the same amount
Neither turns it
They turn it by equal amounts in opposite directions
One turns it and the other does not

items.explain: Herschel found that mirror-image quartz crystals rotate linear polarization by equal amounts in opposite directions.

items.prompt: Sucrose syrup is split into glucose and fructose. Why is the result called invert sugar?

options.label: It turns the syrup upside down in the jar
It makes the syrup sourer
It dissolves the sugar crystals
Its rotation of polarized light flips from right to left

items.explain: Fructose is even more strongly levorotatory than glucose is dextrorotatory, so the conversion makes the direction of rotation go from right to left.
